Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Education | National Parents must consult teachers before pushing gifted children to skip classes – NIM Executive Secretary Source : Kareen Tei 28 November 2026 9:50am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Executive Secretary of the National Interest Movement, Susan Adu-Amankwah, has cautioned against parents unilaterally deciding that their children are gifted and pushing for them to skip classes, warning that such decisions could leave children struggling academically and socially.
She says a child’s intellectual ability alone should not determine whether they are ready to advance to a higher class, as emotional maturity and the ability to cope independently must also be considered.
Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, November 28, she said parents who believe their children are gifted should engage teachers early to have their abilities assessed and their progress monitored within the education system.
Mrs Adu-Amankwah questioned the practice of parents insisting their children are capable of skipping classes even when teachers believe they may not be sufficiently prepared to handle the demands of the next level.
“Sometimes the teacher is saying that, yes, your child is good, but not that good and not good enough to go and pass. And even sometimes, if they are intelligent and good enough to go, they may not be emotionally mature enough to go to a class with other children,” she said, stressing that academic ability alone should not be the basis for determining whether a child is ready to skip a class.
She expressed concern that some children who are pushed into higher classes at a young age struggle with basic responsibilities and independence, particularly when they get to secondary school.
Recounting an experience at her former secondary school, she said she once questioned a teacher about the poor state of cleanliness at the institution, which was previously known for its neatness.
The teacher, she said, attributed the situation partly to the age of some pupils, who were too young to properly take care of themselves, including washing their clothes and keeping their rooms clean.
Mrs Adu-Amankwah said advancing children beyond their developmental readiness could leave them struggling to cope with the demands of boarding school life.
Mrs Adu-Amankwah advised parents who suspect their children are gifted to raise the issue with schools early, rather than waiting until they reach Junior High School to demand that they skip classes.
“If you actually think your child is gifted, you should have noticed it from whatever… You don't wait till the child gets to a JSS and decide that my child is gifted,” she said.
She explained that early engagement with teachers could allow exceptionally gifted pupils to be identified and, where appropriate, advanced within the education system, including skipping certain classes, while ensuring they are adequately prepared for the next stage.
She maintained that the interests of the child must remain paramount in decisions about academic advancement, cautioning that forcing pupils into higher classes without considering their emotional and practical readiness could ultimately do them more harm than good.
